candidates.title: The moon might be hiding a history of ancient supernova explosions
candidates.raw_excerpt: It's now possible to disentangle the sprinkling of supernova dust on the moon from the lunar dirt it is mixed up in, thanks to a new computer model that opens up the moon's surface as a time capsule holding details about the history of supernova explosions near the Earth as our solar system has travelled through space while orbiting the galaxy. When stars explode as a supernova , they shower space with debris, some of which is in the form of radioactive isotopes traveling at high velocity. Some of these radioisotopes enter the solar system to fall on all the planets and moons, including Earth and its moon. Studies of radioisotopes in deep-sea sediments on Earth, coupled with those found in samples of lunar dirt – what scientists term 'regolith' – brought back by the Apollo missions, point to two recent peaks in supernova activity, 2.3 and 7.3 million years ago. "I think it's beautiful that the remains of past stars can be used to navigate the vast history of our Earth – moon neighborhood, if we have knowledge of how to read the stardust," said planetary scientist Emily Costello, of the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, in a statement . However, because of the process of erosion and subduction through plate tectonics, most Earth-bound records of supernova activity in our cosmic neighborhood have been lost and reliable records on Earth only go back about 10 million years. Earth's moon, however, is a different story. Because the moon has no atmosphere, there's no wind or rain erosion, nor are there any plate tectonics. The moon, therefore, should host a record of supernova activity going back 80–100 million years, or even longer. However, while the moon lacks Earth's style of erosion, it does experience what planetary scientists refer to as 'impact gardening'. This is when impacts of objects ranging in size from microscopic micrometeorites to large asteroids , turns over the regolith, mixing it all up including the radioactive supernova debris. candidates.title: New Chinese chip processes hyperspectral imaging instantly
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Chinese researchers have developed a new chip that enables real‑time hyperspectral imaging analysis, cutting out bulky servers and huge data files. 

Hyperspectral imaging identifies what things are made of. Every material reflects, absorbs and emits light differently across the electromagnetic spectrum. Hyperspectral imaging captures this unique "spectral fingerprint," making it vital for remote sensing and industrial inspection. But the extra spectral dimension comes with a cost: massive data. 

The work, led by a team from the Beijing Institute of Technology (BIT), was recently published in the journal Science.

"A single image can take up hundreds of megabytes or even gigabytes, placing huge pressure on back‑end data processing," said Bian Liheng, a tenured professor at BIT.

The team tackled the problem on two fronts. In 2024, they miniaturized the bulky optical system of traditional hyperspectral cameras down to chip level. Now, they've solved the back‑end real‑time computing bottleneck, by mining data correlations to cut redundant calculations, and redesigning the chip's arithmetic units to process data continuously on a single chip.

The breakthrough could transform satellite remote sensing. "When computing is chip‑based, data no longer needs to be transmitted to the ground for processing – satellites can produce results in real time, right on board," Bian said. 

This innovation shifts hyperspectral imaging from offline post‑processing to on‑site real‑time computing, opening new possibilities for portable, embedded systems across a wide range of applications.

candidates.title: China strikes gold – and copper – in deep-earth hunt
candidates.raw_excerpt:
China has hit upon a major gold and copper find in Chating, Xuancheng City, east China's Anhui Province, a discovery that could pave the way for a massive new resource base, the Ministry of Natural Resources said on Tuesday.

The Chating copper-gold deposit, in the heart of the Yangtze River Delta, is one of the country's most promising recent finds with the potential to reach ultra-large scale.

Exploration of deep ore bodies is ongoing, but the mother lode identified so far is about 1.2 kilometers long and 1.1 kilometers wide.

Preliminary estimates suggest potential copper resources could exceed several large-scale deposits, each over 500,000 tonnes. Potential gold veins could top more than 10 large deposits containing over 20 tonnes each. Those numbers are expected to grow as exploration continues.

Hu Xianqi, director of the Geological Exploration Division, said the Chating project is one of the ministry's key explorations for 2026, and the breakthrough, achieved in just months, is significant.

"China's demand for copper is strong. External supply reliance is high, but domestic exploration potential is enormous. Chating is a vivid example," Hu said. 

Copper is essential for solar, wind and new energy vehicles. Once developed, the Chating deposit could supply raw materials to smelting and processing industries in eastern China, helping ease regional shortages.

The discovery is also expected to boost resource supply across the Yangtze River Delta and China's eastern economic belt, supporting regional integration.

candidates.title: NASA, ESA astronauts conduct spacewalk outside ISS
candidates.raw_excerpt:
NASA astronaut Jessica Meir and European Space Agency (ESA) astronaut Sophie Adenot concluded a spacewalk outside the International Space Station (ISS) on Tuesday for spacecraft navigation, scientific research and station maintenance.

The duo began the spacewalk at 8:40 a.m. Eastern Time (1240 GMT). During the 6-hour, 49-minute spacewalk, Meir and Adenot installed a new retroflector on the forward port of the space station's Harmony module to support spacecraft navigation during rendezvous and docking operations.

The duo replaced a high-definition camera on the station's truss and collected a swab of the space station's exterior for microorganisms. They also partially completed work to install jumper cables for electrical systems and started work to prepare for the replacement of the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer's heat-rejecting radiator on a future spacewalk, according to NASA.

During the spacewalk, Adenot experienced some mobility issues with her left arm. Meir inspected Adenot's spacesuit and determined that the glove heater harness was likely getting caught and restricting movement in the left shoulder joint. Unzipping the joint appeared to resolve the issue before the crew entered the airlock, according to NASA.

It was Meir's seventh and Adenot's third spacewalk, also the 284th spacewalk in support of ISS assembly, maintenance and upgrades.

candidates.title: EU questions dozens of companies using new AI powers
candidates.raw_excerpt:
The European Union (EU) said on Tuesday it had begun to use new powers to regulate artificial intelligence (AI) by sending information requests to dozens of companies after incidents this summer highlighted the risks the technology poses.

The European Commission gained new regulatory powers last month under the AI Act, the world's most far-reaching rules to curb potentially dangerous uses of the technology. It entered into force in 2024, with obligations kicking in over several years.

The Commission said on Tuesday it had sent requests for information to more than 30 companies operating in the AI sector.

The requests are a preliminary step before the possible launch of a formal investigation into whether companies are respecting European laws.

"Our goal is to ensure that AI in Europe is developed, released and used safely and transparently," Henna Virkkunen, the Commission's vice president for tech sovereignty and security said in a LinkedIn post over the weekend.

"And we are ready to take all necessary steps to ensure that companies comply with their obligations under the AI Act," she added.

The Commission did not identify the companies to which it sent letters, although Virkkunen said in her post they are located across the world.

Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier said the questionnaires concerned mostly safety and respect of copyright.

A series of incidents in recent months highlighted the risks the most advanced AI models now pose.

candidates.title: Scientists trace 7 stages of a meteorite's life, from hurtling space rock to Earth's surface
candidates.raw_excerpt: Studying 75 meteorites falling to Earth, scientists have identified the seven stages a space rock goes through as it crashes through our atmosphere, each of which is determined by different physical processes. The research found that there are more factors than mere evaporation that determine how fragments of asteroids and comets lose mass and speed passing through the atmosphere before slamming into the ground as meteorites. As well as just "burning up" in the atmosphere, space rocks also go through periods of melting and fragmentation that occur at different altitudes. Aside from shining light on the life cycles of meteorites, the team's research could help us better understand what would happen if a large, potentially hazardous asteroid were to enter Earth's atmosphere. "We used to think that solid rocks would evaporate from the enormous heat and brilliant light generated in the air collision," team leader Peter Jenniskens of the SETI Institute and NASA Ames Research Center said in a statement . "We found instead that first melting and then fragmentation control how a rock loses mass." Seven stages to Earthfall The first stage, phase 1, identified by the team, begins high in Earth's atmosphere . The falling space rock creates a shock wave in front of it that heats it and the gas surrounding it. This turns the falling space rock into a " shooting star " streaking across the sky. Phase 2 begins when the fragment reaches denser air, and the meteor begins to brighten. At this stage, astronomers can determine how the rock is spinning based upon changes in brightness. This brightening continues until phase 3, at which point the space rock becomes a fireball . The team found that it is at this stage that the falling rock loses the most mass via melting. This happens as air flows rapidly around the rock and pulls away melted matter, leaving a trail of droplets that continue to evaporate. An illustration of a fireball streaking across the sky. (Image credit: Shutterstock)

candidates.title: Researchers Alarmed as GPS Readings Suddenly Veer Off by 33 Feet, Enough to Crash Self-Driving Cars
candidates.raw_excerpt: In November of last year, scientists warned of a “severe” solar storm , the strongest in over two decades, colliding with the Earth. Solar storms are the result of a surge in solar activity, with the Sun unleashing a barrage of charged particles that can trigger spectacular auroras — and wreak havoc with communications satellites and radio signals — when they reach the Earth’s magnetosphere. Beyond being ferocious enough to delay the launch of a Mars-bound NASA spacecraft , the storm wreaked absolute havoc with GPS systems back on the ground for hours at a time. As detailed in a new paper published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters , a team of scientists found that global navigation satellite systems experienced “significant positioning errors” of over 33 feet during the superstorm, “large enough to disrupt precision agriculture and autonomous transportation industries” across the continental United States. That’s enough risk to warrant a careful study on these types of events can impact human activity on Earth. “The results underscore the importance of accurate understanding of various space weather phenomena to enhance our predictive capabilities through coordinated observations and physics‐based modeling and ultimately reducing disruptions to RF applications during space weather events,” the paper reads. The researchers analyzed observations from several scientific instruments spread out across the US to watch the chaos unfold last November. The Aurora Oval, a ring-shaped area of pronounced activity around the Earth’s geomagnetic north pole where auroras conventionally occur, was pushed south toward the equator. This triggered a “horizontally extended band of intense density gradients” in the upper atmosphere, causing fluctuations in how long signals take to travel through it. candidates.title: Nonprofit wants to launch 80,000-year mission to Alpha Centauri in 2029 (video)
candidates.raw_excerpt: The first dedicated mission to another star will launch before the end of the decade, if all goes according to plan. A nonprofit called the Fermi Explorer Mission announced today (Sept. 1) that it plans to send a small probe toward Alpha Centauri by 2029. But none of us will live to see the interstellar spacecraft 's historic arrival; its journey is expected to take about 80,000 years. "We hope to be both the first to leave and the last to arrive at Alpha Centauri," Philip Johnston, co-founder and president of the Fermi Explorer Mission, said in a statement today. "None of us will be here when this journey ends, and that is the point. It's about taking the first achievable step and inspiring future generations to keep pushing beyond the limits we inherited." Artist's impression of the planned Fermi Explorer Mission spacecraft, which is targeted to launch toward Alpha Centauri by 2029. (Image credit: Fermi Explorer Mission) Johnston is also co-founder and CEO of Starcloud, a company that plans to operate data centers in space . He started the Fermi Explorer Mission with fellow Starcloud co-founders Ezra Feilden and Adi Oldean. Former U.S. Air Force officer Garrett Jamison leads day-to-day execution of the project. Some big names in the spaceflight world have signed on as advisors, including former Blue Origin president Rob Meyerson and Matt Gialich, co-founder and CEO of the asteroid-mining company AstroForge . The Fermi Explorer project is ambitious but achievable, according to Johnston and his colleagues. They want to launch a spacecraft to the three-star Alpha Centauri system — the sun's nearest stellar neighbor, at about 4.4 light-years away — by 2029. This directed trajectory will be a first. Though NASA's Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft are in interstellar space , they're not headed toward any particular star; rather, they're journeying outward on the path they took to complete their "grand tour" of Jupiter , Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. candidates.title: Flock Is in Major Trouble
candidates.raw_excerpt: As backlash against surveillance grows, governments overseeing cities, townships, and counties around the US are dropping their Flock contracts at a record pace — a retreat so widespread that some say it could affect the company’s viability. The police tech company, known for its sprawling network of automatic license plate readers (ALPRs), has become one of the flashpoints for the country’s revulsion at AI infrastructure, joining data centers and drone-as-first-responder programs as symbols — and targets — of a rising AI dystopia. According to reporting by TechSpot , some 214 municipal governments have opted to drop previously-held contracts with Flock since 2021. That data comes courtesy of Secure Justice, an anti-surveillance group based out of Oakland, California. Just across August, Secure Justice analysis found that some 90 local administrations dropped or non-renewed Flock contracts, quadruple the number of cancellations across July, and a rate of three per day across the whole month. And as cancellations increase, the hit to Flock’s collective utility — not to mention the company’s bottom line — only becomes more pronounced. That’s because Flock offers police the ability to reference data collected by ALPRs belonging not only to other law enforcement agencies, but also to commercial and individual contractees as well. Recent history has shown that when Flock cameras in neighboring towns go down, police become much more likely to cancel or non-renew their own contracts, as the main utility for law enforcement comes from the combined network, rather than just those ALPRs local to one jurisdiction (granted, police officers have often used that network to stalk women instead of actually fighting crime , but that’s another story.) candidates.title: US Military in Chaos as Trump Shares AI Video of Nonexistent Attack on Iran
candidates.raw_excerpt: President Donald Trump sowed a fair bit of confusion after posting not one but two AI-generated videos of a supposed US strike on Iran’s Kharg Island. Trump, as it turned out, was simply hallucinating a fantasy, forcing a US official to clarify Monday that the depicted “attacks” on the island, Iran’s main hub of oil exports, hadn’t actually occurred, The Independent reported . Trump made no effort to clarify that the videos were AI-generated when he posted them on Truth Social. In his first post, made on Sunday night, he only wrote in the caption: “Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!!” Both of the videos are made to look like they were taken from inside a helicopter as the island is engulfed in explosions and flames. He posted the follow-up video just a minute after the first, which is probably a sign of just how much of a kick Trump gets out of living out his fantasies in AI slop; he couldn’t settle for posting just one. candidates.title: On this day in space! Sept. 1, 1979: NASA's Pioneer 11 probe becomes 1st spacecraft to visit Saturn
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Sept. 1, 1979, NASA's robotic space probe Pioneer 11 became the first spacecraft to fly by Saturn . Pioneer 11 launched in 1973 on a mission to explore the asteroid belt, Jupiter and Saturn. It launched directly toward Jupiter , then used Jupiter's gravity to slingshot around the planet, make a sharp turn and start flying toward Saturn. Four years and nine months later, it finally made it to Saturn . During its closest approach, it was about 13,000 miles (2,100 kilometers) above the planet's cloud tops. Because NASA's two Voyager probes were also on their way to Saturn at that point, they sent Pioneer 11 straight through Saturn's rings so it could determine whether it was safe for the Voyagers to do the same thing years down the road. So Pioneer 11 pioneered the way through Saturn's outer rings, going where no spacecraft had gone before — and nearly colliding with a small moon along the way. Pioneer 11 actually discovered several moons, along with a new ring, and the first evidence of a magnetic field around Saturn . Why it mattered An artist's illustration of Pioneer 11 at Saturn, a space first in 1979. (Image credit: NASA) Pioneer 11 may have made history as the first spacecraft to visit Saturn, but its original mission was aimed at a very different planet. The spacecraft was actually the twin of NASA's Pioneer 10 probe, which launched toward Jupiter in March 1972 on a mission to prove spacecraft could survive passage through the asteroid belt and the harsh radiation environment at Jupiter. NASA wanted to be sure because of its next two missions, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 , which it hoped to launch on a tour of the outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune) due to a once-in-175-year alignment of the planets. But before the Voyagers could launch in 1977, Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11 had to make the voyage to at least one of those outer planets first. Their target: Jupiter. candidates.title: Why do black hole flares die out? It may be down to how stars spin
candidates.raw_excerpt: Some stars encounter supermassive black holes and live to tell the tale. New research shows why the flares these encounters cause dim over repeated episodes, and it may be down to the way these stars spin and an escaping binary partner that leaves them to be a stellar snack for a black hole. Some stars are unfortunate enough to encounter the supermassive black holes that sit at the heart of every galaxy, being subjected to immense tidal forces that turn them into a strand of stellar spaghetti, a process called " spaghettification ." This plasma pasta wraps around the black hole and is gradually fed to it, with some former star stuff being ejected as near-light-speed jets. These occurrences are called tidal disruption events (TDEs). However, other stars get a reprieve, passing close enough to a supermassive black hole for the cosmic titan to take a bite and strip off material, but not close enough to be fully destroyed. As the star orbits the supermassive black hole, it takes repeated "bites," with this stellar snacking called a repeating partial tidal disruption event (rpTDE). Each incident causes a flare of light from the vicinity of the black hole , as would be expected from the brightening seen during a standard TDE. But a strange pattern has emerged in rpTDES; each successive flare can become dimmer. Scientists have struggled to explain this dimming for some time, but finally a team of researchers from Syracuse University may have solved this puzzle. To reach an answer to black hole flare dimming, the team considered a factor that hadn't been thought of before: the spin of the star itself. This element explained the dimming of black hole flaring and also helped to explain why not all rpTDEs play out the same. "We were puzzled by this for two years," team leader Ananya Bandopadhyay of Syracuse University said in a statement. candidates.title: Employees Absolutely Loath AI in the Workplace, Survey Finds

candidates.title: China's FAST telescope sheds new light on cosmic evolution
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Scientists have long grappled with a perplexing question: in the early universe, new stars appeared with dazzling frequency, yet today, star formation has clearly slowed. Now, a new study led by Chinese scientists is offering fresh and crucial clues to help unravel this cosmic mystery.

An international team, including the National Astronomical Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NAOC), the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory (SHAO) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and other institutions, has made significant progress on this front. Using China's Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) together with the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), a global project involving more than 70 institutions, the researchers conducted high-precision measurements of neutral hydrogen evolution in the universe over the past 4.5 billion years. Their work is shedding new light on this long-standing puzzle.

"Why is it becoming increasingly difficult for the universe to form new stars? This is a core question in the field of galaxy formation and evolution," said Jiang Peng, a researcher at NAOC. A widely held and intuitive explanation is that as the universe evolves, the cold gas that nurtures stars is gradually consumed, eventually leading to the decline in star formation. If this scenario holds, then the drop in the star formation rate should inevitably be accompanied by a commensurate depletion of cold gas reservoirs.

candidates.title: Experts: What makes the Gyirong Port rescue so difficult?
candidates.raw_excerpt:
A massive mudslide triggered by a glacier collapse in Nepal struck Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on August 26. Rescue teams are racing against time to search for the missing, clear debris and monitor the barrier lake. But the operation is exceptionally difficult. What makes the rescue at Gyirong Port so challenging?

A cascading disaster with extraordinary destructive force

This was far more than an ordinary mudslide. An ice-rock avalanche at an altitude of about 5,200 meters in Nepal swept down more than 3,000 meters toward Gyirong Port, which sits at an elevation of about 1,800 to 2,000 meters. Along the way, it picked up huge amounts of loose material, forming a high-speed debris flow that eventually swept into Gyirong Port.

The resulting ice-rock debris flow traveled about 22 kilometers at an average speed of around 50 meters per second, according to Liu Weiming, a researcher at the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment under the Chinese Academy of Sciences and the Ministry of Water Resources.

Rescuers are not dealing with simply "a flow of mud and water." Instead, they are confronting a cascading process in which each stage of the disaster intensified the next, said Dai Zili, deputy secretary-general of the International Consortium on Geo-disaster Reduction.

As the ice and rock moved down the valley, they eroded the surrounding slopes and swept up loose deposits that had accumulated in the mountains. More than 30 million cubic meters of material was ultimately involved, Dai noted.

candidates.title: Without new landers or rovers, it's helicopters or bust for NASA's Mars program
candidates.raw_excerpt: For the first time in more than 30 years, NASA has no firm plans to send any new landers or rovers to Mars. Instead, the agency's near-term focus at the red planet is on aerial drones, a pioneering mode of exploration that didn't seem realistic until a few years ago. The first real use of drones for science at Mars will come with the SkyFall mission, a fleet of three helicopters set for launch as soon as late 2028. SkyFall's helicopters will ride to the red planet with NASA's Space Reactor-1 "Freedom" mission , which has the primary objective of demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in deep space. The launch schedule is aggressive for SR-1 Freedom and SkyFall, projects that didn't even exist in NASA's portfolio six months ago. NASA's plan for the SR-1 Freedom mission, estimated to cost $2.1 billion, calls for repurposing the core module of the canceled Gateway lunar space station into a testbed for nuclear electric propulsion. SkyFall will build on NASA's success with the Ingenuity helicopter, an experimental vehicle that became the first rotorcraft to fly on another world in 2021. Read full article Comments

candidates.raw_excerpt: There are, by various estimates, several trillion planets within what is known as the Local Group of galaxies—our closest galaxy neighbors, including our own Milky Way. Many of these planets are within the habitable zone of their stars. So if life finds a way, where are the alien civilizations? This is the crux of what is known as the Fermi paradox , which posits that if life is fairly common in the Universe, humans should have collected credible evidence for the existence of extraterrestrial civilizations by now. People who think about this paradox believe there may be some "filter" that limits or entirely prevents an advanced civilization from sending out probes or even life-bearing spacecraft to nearby stars. Philip Johnston is someone who thinks a lot about the Fermi paradox. A mathematician and physicist from the United Kingdom, Johnston has gained some notoriety lately in the space community as one of the biggest proponents of orbital data centers. He co-founded Starcloud in 2024 to develop such data centers, and the company is presently valued at $2.3 billion. Read full article Comments

candidates.title: SCO's ecological partnership: Protecting species, restoring ecosystems
candidates.raw_excerpt:
From the high mountains where snow leopards roam to the shrinking landscapes of the Aral Sea, Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) countries are joining hands to tackle ecological challenges through cooperation and shared solutions. As one of the world's most biodiverse countries and one of the first parties to sign and ratify the Convention on Biological Diversity, China is deepening cooperation with regional partners to advance biodiversity protection and environmental restoration.

Protecting 'king of snow mountains'

The snow leopard, known as the "king of the snow mountains," inhabits high-altitude areas from Central Asia to the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau and the Mongolian Plateau. Many SCO member states are home to the species.

Against the backdrop of climate change and the global biodiversity crisis, protecting snow leopards is critical to maintaining ecosystem stability. SCO countries and broader Asian range countries have agreed to work together to conserve the species and the natural ecosystem they depend on.

Cooperation dates back to October, 2013, when 12 snow leopard range countries, including China, gathered at the first Global Snow Leopard Conservation Forum in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. They signed the Bishkek Declaration on the Conservation of the Snow Leopard, and launched the Global Snow Leopard and Ecosystems Protection Program (GSLEP) to implement the commitments.

candidates.title: FBI Now Allowing History of Bestiality Among New Recruits
candidates.raw_excerpt: The Federal Bureau of Investigation looks almost unrecognizable under director Kash Patel’s leadership. The agency’s head has been embroiled in a seemingly endless list of controversies, from allegations of excessive drinking to buying up location data on everyday American citizens to furthering of harebrained conspiracies . Patel lacked virtually any degree of relevant working experience for the job before the Senate confirmed him — and now, the agency is opening the doors for even more highly questionable hirings. As inside sources told CBS News , the FBI has quietly lowered standards of its background checks for potential federal agents and other personnel. The bureau is now officially looking the other way when it comes to prostitution, for instance — as long as recruits didn’t hire sex workers over three times. Even more eyebrow-raising is that the FBI is even allowing the consideration of candidates who engaged in bestiality or animal cruelty, according to CBS ‘ sources. However, any such incidents would’ve had to have taken place before the candidate turned 18. The broadcaster’s sources also said there was no distinction between candidates who were forced into sexual activity with animals or if they did so willingly. candidates.title: Marijuana Factory Explodes, Causing Two Deaths
candidates.raw_excerpt: Two are dead and over 25 buildings damaged after a cataclysmic explosion at a cannabis facility in Sand Springs, Oklahoma last week. According to initial reporting by KTUL , the blast happened at 1:30am, and literally blew the roof off the building, sending out shockwaves that could be felt up to 30 to 40 miles away . “It was like around 1:20, 1:25. And it was just a big boom,” local man Donovan Ruffin, who lives a mile away from the blast, told the news channel. “Me and my wife woke up at the same time. And as soon as I heard it, I woke up… I have a window right by my bed, so I seen a flash.” Ryan Bassham, the owner of the THC facility where the explosion occurred, was later arrested on murder charges, People reported , after defying an order from the fire marshal to halt extraction operations. One explanation being offered up — though not officially confirmed — is that the explosion traces back to the use of butane to produce THC concentrate. One of the more popular methods by which the cannabis industry produces concentrated products like rosin is through a process known as butane hash oil (BHO) extraction. Basically, producers use liquid butane as a solvent, pouring it over raw plants at temperatures in the ballpark of -40 degrees Fahrenheit. Because liquid butane has an exceptionally low boiling point — 30.02 degrees Fahrenheit to be exact — the solvent can be easily cooked off after mixing with the plant matter, leaving just the dissolved cannabinoids behind. Though this is said to be one of the most straightforward methods for concentrating cannabis, the use of highly flammable butane makes it one of the most dangerous. As the publisher Technology Networks explained in a blog post on BHO extraction, a “faulty gasket or improper check could lead to disaster.” Overall, there is no national count of BHO-related explosions or injuries, so it’s difficult to say how common an occurrence it is. candidates.title: Billionaire Coinbase CEO Boasts That He Would Never Donate to Charity
candidates.raw_excerpt: There was a time in the United States when the richest moguls, regardless of their many personal shortcomings, embraced philanthropy in a cynical effort to keep the angry mobs at bay. Andrew Carnegie famously built libraries, John D Rockefeller helped fund research that eventually eradicated hookworm, while JP Morgan donated vast collections of art and books to museums and other cultural institutions. Today’s robber barons aren’t in such a giving mood. Sure, there are some figures like Microsoft’s Bill Gates — who has plenty of his own problems , to be clear — but they seem to be quickly becoming the minority. Case in point, the billionaire CEO of cyrpto-trading company Coinbase, Brian Armstrong, recently went on a tirade about how charity is actually a “net negative on the world.” “The common view is that philanthropy is a noble cause,” Amstrong said during a recent appearance on the right-wing Katie Miller Podcast . “And like, Bill Gates after the DoJ thing is like, ‘I’m going to go rehabilitate my image, I’m going to do philanthropy.'” That’s a fool’s errand to Armstrong, however, as such philanthropic aspirations — selfish as they are — can become “captured by ideology.” “I guess I have sort of a contrarian view where a lot of charities and philanthropies are actually net negative on the world,” Armstrong continued. “And they get captured. It’s actually remarkably hard to find a foundation that has not gotten captured by ideology.” Though Amstrong’s estimated net worth of around $8.7 billion puts him in the top 1 percent of the top 1 percent, he says that “so far, I’ve just been like ‘I’m not going to do that.’ “ More on tech billionaires: AI Billionaires Are So Greedy That They’re Supercharging Sales of Yachts and Private Jets The post Billionaire Coinbase CEO Boasts That He Would Never Donate to Charity appeared first on Futurism .

candidates.title: The Music Industry’s New Lawsuit Against Anthropic Should Have Dario Amodei Shivering With Fear
candidates.raw_excerpt: Dario Amodei’s Anthropic is facing yet another massive legal challenge. Sony Music and Warner, both juggernauts in the music publishing industry, filed a major lawsuit against the AI company late Friday night, accusing it of “one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history.” More specifically, the publishers said that Anthropic had, without permission, trained its AI models on “tens of thousands” of copyrighted compositions, asking for remuneration up to $150,000 per work, in addition to up to $25,000 for each time Anthropic intentionally stripped copyright data. As The Verge points out , that means damages could reach several billion dollars. While the latest lawsuit is far from the first time a frontier AI lab has been accused of copyright infringement, this particular suit could be very difficult for Amodei and Anthropic to defend against. That’s because the suit names the exact same dataset of pirated works that Anthropic cofounder Benjamin Mann — who is listed as a defendant — was found to have illegally downloaded, culminating in the blockbuster $1.5 billion settlement in September 2025. “Among the many millions of books that Defendants torrented from these illegal pirate websites were books containing the lyrics and sheet music to hundreds or more of Music Publishers’ copyrighted musical compositions,” the latest legal filing reads. The works include massive hits like Bon Jovi’s “Livin’ on a Prayer,” Earth, Wind & Fire’s “September,” and Leonard Cohen’s “Hallelujah,” according to the suit. “Defendants Anthropic and its founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann have conducted a brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works on a massive scale in order to develop, operate, and reap enormous profits from Anthropic’s ‘Claude’ series of artificial intelligence models,” the suit reads. candidates.title: Google Maps Rival Surges In Popularity After It Refuses to Rename Lake Ontario
candidates.raw_excerpt: When president Donald Trump, in his latest paroxysm, declared that he would be renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” Google instantly capitulated. So eager was it to realize his will that it actually renamed the lake before official government map makers did, Ars Technica noted . No one really expected a tech monopoly to take a principled stand against the decision, but you might’ve expected it to at least pretend that it was deliberating acting on an order with real diplomatic ramifications . But that’s not what Google did, and its rivals are now thanking it. MapQuest, the self-styled “OG of online mapping” that your mom probably used to print out before family roadtrips, announced defiantly on social media Thursday that it wouldn’t be changing the name of Lake Ontario. The posts garnered hundreds of thousands of likes on platforms including Instagram and X, and these viral moments seem to be translating into actual success. As TechCrunch reports , MapQuest’s mobile app has consequently surged in popularity, rising its way to becoming the number one navigation app in all of the US on Apple’s App Store. It’s become so popular, in fact, that it also climbed to the fourth position on the App Store’s Top Charts, which excludes games, and number eight overall across apps and games. Canadians approve of MapQuest’s stand, too. Across the northern border, it reached number two overall as of Sunday evening, per TechCrunch . As they say: do nothing, win . “We’re not changing it,” MapQuest declared in the viral post , with a screenshot of a map showing Lake Ontario. Clearly relishing the moment, MapQuest made another dig days later. “We are aware that Lake Ontario is being correctly labeled on our map,” it posted . In numbers, the surge is pretty impressive, too. TechCrunch cites data from the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower which shows that MapQuest saw 184,000 global downloads during the week of August 24, which is a more than ten-fold increase week-over-week. candidates.title: Data Center Backlash Has Officially Rattled Sam Altman
candidates.raw_excerpt: The AI industry has lost an astonishing amount of goodwill with the public. Once seen as exciting new tech that could make our lives easier and better, the construction of countless new data centers to support power-hungry AI models has soured the mood considerably. Protesters are waging a war against $130 billion in data center investments, arguing they’re only benefiting a select few wealthy individuals, while threatening water supplies , driving up the cost of living , and churning out incomprehensible amounts of pollution . Even OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has caught on to the backlash, as it slowly dawns him and his fellow executives that the vast majority of Americans want nothing to do with them. “Clearly, people hate data centers — right now, at least,” Altman told Time in a new interview. “People are pretty negative on AI.” Caught between a rock and a hard place, rattled CEOs are now caught trying to appeal to lawmakers for favorable regulations as their constituents coalesce into a bipartisan movement against data centers. Some, like Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg , are holding onto their guns, painting a rosy picture of a future in which we no longer have to work and live a life of leisure thanks to AI. Others, like Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian , are desperately looking for a way to sell the public on data centers — a gargantuan task, considering the sheer scale of the fallout. For Altman, the topic is particularly personal. Earlier this year, a man threw a molotov cocktail at his house just days before it was struck by gunfire . In the case of the former, the man was accused of trying to firebomb the executive’s home repeatedly warned that AI will exterminate humankind and was associated with a political movement called PauseAI, which is calling for more oversight over AI safety. “It has been a painful personal experience,” Altman told Time . candidates.title: Alarming Study Suggests That Using AI Is Turning Humans More Robotic
candidates.raw_excerpt: Now that AI models have officially passed the Turing Test , there’s no doubt that they’re capable of imitating human traits — at least in text form — to a degree that would have flabbergasted even an expert just few years back. After all, large language models are built by digesting copious amounts of human-authored content, making them little more than algorithms that mirror our behavior back at us. But the more we use AI tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude, those tables are starting to turn: chatbots appear to be influencing human behavior making us behave more like them — a terrifying thought as the tech plays an ever-greater role in our lives. As detailed in a new paper in the journal AI & Society , designed to build out a new framework and start a discussion, an international team of researchers suggested that the use of AI chatbots, specifically in customer service settings, could be making humans act more robotic even as bots become more like us. “As generative systems and socially responsive service agents enter everyday consumption, human-AI interaction increasingly resembles a quasi-social encounter rather than a utilitarian interface,” they wrote. The researchers introduced a new concept called “robotoid humanness” to put a name to the “emergent drift in which consumers come to experience themselves as most fluent, correct, or socially viable when they become compatible with machine legibility, machine pacing, and machine logic.” Put differently, it’s a “bidirectional influence, where robots become more like people, and people become more like robots,” said coauthor University of Birmingham marketing researcher Inci Toral-Manson in a statement about the work . candidates.title: Spotify and YouTube Profiles of Legendary Jazz Musicians Hijacked by AI Waifu Spam
candidates.raw_excerpt: William “Sonny” Criss was the consummate working musician. Having started on the saxophone at 11 years old, Criss began his professional career filling in on gigs with bandleader Johnny Otis, before going on to play alongside jazz legends like Charlie Parker, Miles Davis, Cole Porter, and Dizzy Gillespie. Though he might never have risen to the level of a household name, his tremendous and ever-evolving output puts him in a league with some of the most celebrated bebop artists of his generation. Today, most will interact with Criss’s music on a streaming service like Spotify or YouTube. Yet as these platforms fail to prevent the onslaught of AI slop, the musician’s streaming profiles are becoming a host for parasitic spam — and unfortunately, he’s not the only one. In addition to Criss, profiles of artists including the vocalist Jean Carne, cornetist Red Nichols, and clarinetist Jimmie Noone have become inundated with various forms of AI spam. On Spotify, YouTube, and Amazon Music, each of these musicians recently picked up “new” singles plastered with AI-generated cover art, uploaded in 2026 and copyrighted to the publisher “Ami bacuk.” Criss’s profile on Spotify, for example, started displatwo brand-new tunes, which is an impressive feat considering he died in 1977. Titled “Tell me why” and “but a heartache,” both feature a generic anime waifu on their cover, and were supposedly composed by “Zainul Irpan,” a mashup of two generic Arabic-rooted names. Though each song is a jazz tune featuring alto sax and a rhythm section, their origin is nearly impossible to trace, as they’re neither rebrands of existing tracks by Criss or identifiable via music ID software. If it weren’t for the jarring mishmash between characteristically laid-back bebop album covers and the bright, colorful anime images, the tunes would be difficult to distinguish from the musician’s original work.
